Abstract
As high performance computing (HPC) moves towards exascale, storage systems face core challenges such as data flood­
ing, bandwidth bottlenecks, mixed load coordination, and performance cost balancing. This article systematically reviews 
the cutting-edge technologies of high performance storage systems, covering four aspects: storage architecture, hardware, 
software, and networking. At the architecture level, storage computing separation, distributed and hierarchical architec­
tures decouple computing and storage resources, and optimize latency and scalability through high-speed networks. Typi­
cal cases include supercomputer systems such as Frontier and Fugaku. In terms of hardware, persistent memory, all flash 
array, and integrated storage and computing chips significantly improve throughput and reduce latency, while ZNS SSD 
and QLC technology optimize cost and lifespan. At the software level, distributed parallel file systems respond to mas­
sive small files and high concurrency access through burst buffering technology. In network communication, low latency 
protocols such as Slingshot, InfiniBand, and RoCE support TB level bandwidth, while CXL technology promotes storage 
resource pooling. In the future, photon interconnection, AI native architecture, and green energy-saving technologies will 
further promote the development of high performance storage towards efficiency and intelligence, to support ZB level 
storage requirements in scenarios such as Exascale computing and AI training.

In view of the problems and challenges faced by the

The storage architecture of high performance stor­
age system refers to the systematic design and organiza­
tion between its hardware, software and protocol layers to 
achieve the ultimate throughput, low latency, scalability and 
reliability. Its core challenge is to solve the bottleneck prob­
lems of traditional storage systems in the scenarios of super 
large-scale computing, AI training, real-time analysis and 
so on. The current solutions are mainly storage computing 
separation architecture (Shu 2023), distributed architecture 
(Zeng and Yunfei 2021), hierarchical architecture (Xiao­
bin et al. 2023), and the cutting-edge development trends 
include near-computing storage architecture (Fujiki et al. 
2023), AI native storage architecture (Tencent Cloud 2024).
The storage hardware of high performance storage refers 
to the special storage device and its interconnection com­
ponents designed to meet the extremely high performance 
requirements, covering the full stack hardware innovation 
from the storage medium to the controller. Its core goal is 
to break through the performance bottleneck of traditional 
hardware and support the demand for massive data access. 
New storage hardware includes persistent memory (Shi and 
Wang 2016), full flash array (Committee 2017), GPU stor­
age technology (NVIDIA 2025b), and is also developing 
towards memory computing integrated chip (Kang et al. 
2024).
The storage software in high performance storage gener­
ally refers to the distributed parallel file system. Its core is to 
store the file data and metadata in multiple nodes, and realize 
the high performance data reading and writing through the 
parallel access mechanism. At present, there are challenges 
and problems such as massive extreme aggregate bandwidth 
(China Metrology Society 2025), metadata bottleneck (Lv 
Wenhao and Youyou 2022), intensive small file operation 
(Yuelong et al. 2012).
The storage network communication of high performance 
storage refers to the special network architecture and proto­
col connecting the computing node and the storage device, 
which aims to achieve very low latency, ultra-high band­
width and reliable data transmission, so as to meet the high-
efficiency storage requirements of massive data in HPC, AI 
training, real-time analysis and other scenarios. Its core goal 
is to eliminate the bottleneck of network transmission and 
ensure that the storage I/O performance matches the com­
puting power. RDMA (Kalia et al. 2016), RoCE (Guo et al. 
2016) and CXL (Al Maruf and Chowdhury 2023; Wang et 
al. 2024) technologies, which have been widely used, have 
broad prospects for development.
In addition, this paper will summarize and prospect the 
development trend and future work of high performance 
storage system based on the core challenges of high perfor­
mance storage system, production system and key technolo­
gies in research work.
1  HPC and HPC storage
1.1  HPC
High performance computing is a technical science of the 
theory, method, technology and application of using high 
performance computers to realize parallel computing. The 
core issue of using the continuously developing high per­
formance architecture and parallel processing units to real­
ize high performance parallel computing is that the research 
scope in this field includes parallel architecture, parallel 
computing model, parallel network communication and 
parallel algorithm design (Liao and Xiao 2016; Sterling et 
al. 2017; Reed et al. 2022). High performance computer 
system is a computer system specially designed to perform 
complex computing tasks. It is usually composed of a large 
number of computing nodes, and has high computing power 
and data processing ability. It is widely used in scientific 
research, engineering design, data analysis, artificial intel­
ligence and other fields to solve large-scale and complex 
computing problems (Licheng et al. 2016; Reed and Don­
garra 2015; Gharakhani and Zohoor 2015; Garcia-Gasulla 
et al. 2020).
High performance computer system is the core infra­
structure to promote scientific and technological progress 
and national competitiveness. In every field of the national 
economy, it plays an irreplaceable role. It has become a key 
path to explore and resolve complex problems in various 
fields, helping industries break through development bottle­
necks and move towards higher quality progress (Kurz et 
al. 2022; Lange et al. 2021; Banchelli et al. 2020; Mizzi et 
al. 2015; Hager and Wellein 2010). In scientific research, it 
helps to reveal the laws of the evolution of the universe and 
accelerate the development of new drugs; In the industrial 
field, it supports intelligent manufacturing, energy optimi­
zation and aerospace design; At the national security level, 
it provides key support for password decoding and nuclear 
weapon simulation. In addition, with the explosive growth

1.2  HPC storage
High performance storage system is a special storage archi­
tecture designed to meet the requirements of massive data 
processing and high performance computing. It has the 
core characteristics of ultra-high throughput, low latency, 
high concurrent access and scalability. Through distributed 
storage, parallel file system and high-speed network com­
munication technology (such as RDMA, NVMe-oF (Bing 
et al. 2024)), it distributes data to multiple nodes and sup­
ports parallel reading and writing. It is widely used in super­
computing center, artificial intelligence training, real-time 
analysis and other fields. Typical solutions include Lustre 
(Lustre File System 2024), Ceph (Ceph Official Website 
2025) and so on, which can achieve terabytes per second 
data transmission and break through the performance bottle­
neck of traditional storage.
High performance storage system is the key infrastructure 
to support modern scientific research and industrial upgrad­
ing. In scientific research, it accelerates the data processing 
of climate simulation, gene sequencing and particle phys­
ics experiments. In the industrial field, it helps the real-time 
decision-making of intelligent manufacturing and automatic 
driving. In the field of artificial intelligence, it provides a 
stable data supply for the training of 100 billion parameter 
models. In addition, as a national strategic resource, it is 
directly related to national defense security and economic 
competitiveness, and is an indispensable “data engine” in 
the digital economy era.
Since the rise of distributed storage (Arpaci-Dusseau and 
Arpaci-Dusseau 2023) in the 1990s, high performance stor­
age technology has continued to evolve. At the beginning 
of the twenty-first century, Lustre, GPFS (IBM 2025) and 
other systems pushed supercomputing storage into the PB 
era; After 2010, the latency of all flash memory array and 
RDMA network will be reduced to microsecond level, and 
exascale computing will be gradually realized. At present, 
the technical focus has shifted to the integration of storage 
and computing, persistent memory and green energy sav­
ing. In the future, photonic interconnection, quantum stor­
age and AI-driven intelligent optimization will reshape the 
storage architecture and support the data flood in the ZB era.
In a word, in the process of moving towards 10E com­
puting, high performance computing puts forward high 
requirements and challenges for the performance of parallel 
storage systems. For a long time, restricted by the mechani­
cal components of the disk, the technical progress of the 
storage system in the supercomputer system has been lag­
ging behind the computing system and interconnection sys­
tem. This imbalance has become more prominent with the 
advent of the era of exascale to 10E computing. With the 
continuous improvement of computing power, the scale of 
problems, and the expansion of supercomputer applications, 
the amount of data generated and processed by the complete 
process of scientific computing, cognitive computing and 
data analysis has increased exponentially, and the growth 
rate is much faster than the performance growth of the stor­
age system, resulting in the calculation and data processing 
efficiency being seriously limited by the ability of data input 
and output. At the same time, traditional supercomputing, 
big data and artificial intelligence will be deeply integrated 
in high performance computers in the future. Data intensive 
and large-scale applications make existing storage systems 
inefficient, limited scalability and low availability under 
the condition of coexistence of large-scale and complex 
I/O modes, posing severe challenges to traditional stor­
age media, storage architecture and storage software. New 
parallel storage architectures and new storage technolo­
gies must be developed to support the efficient operation of 
future 10E computers.

traditional storage, so as to meet the stringent requirements 
for data access speed, scale and reliability in the fields of 
scientific computing, artificial intelligence and big data 
analysis. From the early centralized storage to the distrib­

2.1  Storage and computing separation and 
distributed architecture
With the development of computing requirements to 10E 
level, high performance storage architecture has experi­
enced a profound change from the integration of storage 
and computing to the separation of storage and computing. 
By decoupling computing resources from storage resources 
and using high-speed network to achieve cross node data 
access, the storage computing separation architecture 
breaks through the expansion bottleneck of the traditional 
tight coupling architecture. The independently expanded 
computing cluster and storage pool not only improve the 
resource utilization efficiency, but also adapt to the require­
ments of dynamic load in high performance environment.
The storage computing separation and distributed archi­
tecture is the mainstream storage architecture of the current 
high performance computer system. As shown in Fig.  1, 
the computing nodes are usually separated from the stor­
age nodes, and the storage nodes are dispersed into multiple 
autonomous units. The horizontal expansion is achieved 
through the separation of metadata and data and load 
balancing.
As shown in Table  1, the top ten high performance 
computer systems in the TOP500 (2024) list all adopt the 
storage-computing separation architecture and distributed 
storage architecture.

2.2  Hierarchical storage architecture
2.2.1  I/O forwarding layer
Most of the storage systems of high performance computing 
before 2010 are composed of a single layer of global shared 
storage system. Computing nodes directly access the global 
shared storage system through the network, such as Jag­
uar (ORNL 2009) and Tianhe-1 (National Supercomputing 
Center in Tianjin 2010). The single-layer storage architec­
ture based on global shared storage is relatively simple and 
easy to share storage resources. It can provide a completely 
consistent file view for each process of parallel programs, 
better alleviate the scalability problem of high concurrent 
I/O, and simplify the development of parallel programs.
With the continuous expansion of the scale of high per­
formance computing system, the traditional single-level 
global shared storage system is facing severe challenges in 
performance, reliability and scalability. When the number 
of computing nodes expands to tens of thousands or even 
hundreds of thousands, the global shared storage system 
needs to process concurrent I/O requests from a large num­
ber of computing nodes, which not only puts forward high

As shown in Fig. 3, take Japan’s Fugaku as an example 
(RIKEN 2024), the system adopts a hierarchical file sys­
tem architecture, including three layers. The first layer is 
the LLIO (lightweight layered IO accelerator) file system 
composed of SSDs deployed on computing nodes. Every 
16 computing nodes corresponds to 1.6 TB of resources. 
Its main function is to bind with specific applications and 
provide I/O acceleration services for these applications. The 
second layer file system is based on Lustre extension and 
is named Fujitsu Exabyte FS. These two-layer file systems 
migrate data through I/O forwarding nodes, which not only 
effectively reduce the running burden of parallel file sys­
tems, but also provide higher transient I/O access perfor­
mance for computing nodes. The third layer file system uses 
the commercial cloud storage system.
The storage architecture of I/O forwarding layer is used 
to realize the decoupling of computing and storage, so that 
storage system, and is composed of a group of special I/O 
nodes. The computing node first sends the I/O request to an 
I/O node in the I/O forwarding layer, and then the I/O node 
completes the specific processing work. Normally, the I/O 
forwarding layer will divide the computing nodes into M 
subsets, each subset contains N computing nodes, and the 
I/O requests of each subset are forwarded by a designated 
I/O node. The client with parallel file system mounted on 
the I/O node is mainly responsible for forwarding the I/O 
request of the computing node to the target storage node of 
the global shared storage system.
In recent years, high performance computers using multi-
layer storage architecture have gradually become the main­
stream. This architecture effectively solves the bottleneck 
problems in scalability and performance of the traditional 
single-layer storage architecture by introducing the I/O for­
warding layer. Typical representatives of multi-layer storage 
architecture include Fugaku in Japan, Summit and Sierra in

In the top ten high performance computer systems, El

also brings flexibility to the system design. For example,

performance, while storage networks can use relatively sim­

addition, the introduction of I/O forwarding layer separates 
the computing network from the storage network, effec­
tively reducing the network size and significantly enhancing 
the overall stability of the system.

In the high performance computer system with large net­
work scale, the network latency caused by network hop, 
routing and switching is difficult to avoid. Even with Infini­
Band HDR (200Gbps), the link bandwidth is still lower than 
the local throughput of the top PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD. The 
training of AI scenarios such as the 100 billion parameter 
model (such as GPT-4) requires high-frequency reading of 
terabytes of data sets, and the metadata latency of traditional

The advent of Persistent Memory (PMEM) necessitated a

AI-driven storage management (Ye et al. 2024) represents a

heterogeneous storage media (e.g., DRAM, PMEM, SSD, 
HDD), moving beyond static heuristic-based policies. The 
key trade-offs among these architectures revolve around the 
balance between consistency, scalability, and tail latency, 
with no one-size-fits-all solution. The future trajectory 
points towards increasingly intelligent, composable, and 
hardware-aware storage architectures that can dynamically 
adapt to workload demands.
3  Storage hardware
3.1  New storage media
With the separation of computing and storage, the latency 
overhead of storage system increases significantly, which 
urges the industry to seek new technical means to optimize 
this problem.
The introduction of new storage media is reshaping the 
storage architecture design of high performance computing. 
Its core goal is to break through the performance limitations 
of traditional hard disk and ordinary SSD through the deep 
matching of media characteristics and computing require­
ments. Persistent memory, such as Intel Optane series, is 
widely used in metadata acceleration scenarios with its 
nanosecond latency and byte addressing capabilities. For 
example, Aurora supercomputing uses Intel Optane devices 
to build a distributed metadata server, which compresses the 
latency of file system directory traversal from milliseconds 
to microseconds, and supports the rapid retrieval of billions 
of files; The persistent memory also supports restarting 
simulation tasks directly from the point of interruption after 
power failure recovery, avoiding the recovery time of sev­
eral hours of the traditional checkpoint mechanism.
The combination of NVMe SSD and ZNS (Hynix 2019) 
technology provides a new optimization path for high 
throughput scenarios. NVMe protocol gives full play to the 
read–write aggregate bandwidth is as high as 75 TB/s and 
35 TB/s.
The main usage methods of the near-computing storage 
layer include serving as the burst buffer layer, the under­
lying file system cache, the temporary file system, etc. As 
a temporary cache, it handles transient high-intensity I/O 
requests in computing tasks, such as 10,000-core checkpoint 
writes. Summit supercomputing uses a burst buffer tempo­
rary storage simulation checkpoint based on IBM spectrum 
scale, with a peak write speed of 2.5 TB/s, and then asyn­
chronously transferred to the back-end storage to reduce the 
global storage pressure. In the AI training data acceleration 
scenario, the training data set can be cached to reduce the 
latency of loading data from remote storage. For example, 
NVIDIA GPU direct storage (NVIDIA 2024b) allows the 
GPU to directly access the NVMe SSD, bypassing CPU 
memory replication. NVIDIA DGX A100 calculates 8 local 
NVME SSDs of the node as the training data set cache, and 
the ResNet-50 training efficiency is improved by 40%.
In addition, the combination of near-computing stor­
age layer and new storage hardware is also a development 
trend. Currently, the latest exascale computing system 
Aurora (Argonne Leadership Computing Facility 2024) in 
the United States will be configured with Intel Optane (Intel

2.3  Prospect
The architecture of high-performance storage systems is 
undergoing a fundamental reconstruction, driven by the end 
of Dennard scaling and the rise of data-intensive workloads. 
This evolution is characterized by a shift from monolithic, 
scale-up designs towards disaggregated and composable

scale-out model, championed by open-source systems like 
Ceph (Ceph Official Website. 2025), uses pseudo-random 
data placement to eliminate central metadata bottlenecks,

4.1  I/o node burst buffer
The I/O node burst buffer technology provides a fast cache 
area for applications by deploying special I/O nodes between 
the computing node and the global shared storage system, 
and configuring the burst buffer layer on these nodes. The 
application program can quickly write checkpoint data or 
other output data to the burst buffer on the I/O node, and 
then the I/O node asynchronously writes these data back 
to the global shared storage system. This process enables 
the application to quickly enter the next computing phase 
without waiting for the data to be completely written to the 
global storage.
The advantage of this scheme is that it does not need 
any modification to the application or the underlying stor­
age system, and because the number of I/O nodes is rela­
tively small, it does not need large-scale deployment of SSD 
devices with high cost. Therefore, shared burst buffer has 
become a cost-effective storage acceleration solution, which 
has been widely used by many supercomputers.
With the gradual decline of SSD price, researchers 
began to explore expanding the deployment scale of SSD 
in supercomputers to further improve the I/O performance 
of high performance computing applications. Among them, 
the most representative solutions include DataWarp (HPE 
2024a) of Cray and IME of DDN (Betke and Kunkel 2018). 
These schemes significantly improve the overall perfor­
mance and efficiency of the system by optimizing the data 
cache and write back mechanism.

storage layer based on SSD by deploying NVMe SSDs on

the underlying global shared storage system. Before the job

storage space through the script command; After the job is 
completed, export the output data to the underlying storage 
direct control of data placement. This host-guided data man­

more predictable latency, and improved device longevity. 
Although Intel Optane Persistent Memory (PMEM) (Jeong 
and Jung 2021) has been discontinued, its legacy is pro­
found; it served as a pioneering implementation of Storage-
Class Memory (SCM), blurring the line between memory 
and storage. It forced the software community to develop 
new programming models and file systems (e.g., NOVA)

Concurrently, the field of Computational Storage (Lukken 
and Trivedi 2021) is gaining traction, embedding process­

tasks like compression, encryption, or data filtering, thereby 
reducing data movement and freeing host CPU resources 
for core application logic. The key trade-offs in storage 
hardware now revolve around the cost-per-bit, endurance, 
performance consistency, and host-managed complexity, 
with different technologies occupying distinct niches in the 
storage hierarchy.

GekkoFS (2024) is a burst buffer project based on local 
resources of computing nodes supported by the EU NEXT­

irrelevant calls to the local file system. The client maintains 
a mapping of file and directory descriptors in the kernel. 
The communication between client and server is realized 
through RPC (remote procedure call). The client distributes 
the data and metadata to all nodes by hash, without main­

metadata. To ensure the load balance of data distribution, 
data requests will be split into equal-sized blocks before 
being distributed to file system nodes. GekkoFS server 
uses key value storage to manage metadata, and completes 
timely file persistence by interacting with local file system. 
The relaxation of consistency and POSIX operation support 
makes GekkoFS perform well in terms of performance and 
scalability.

ports the high performance I/O requirements of large-scale

4.2  Near-computing burst buffer
Distributed burst buffer technology is realized by directly 
configuring high-speed storage devices on computing or 
near-computing nodes. Teng Wang et al. proposed a file sys­
tem based on local resources – BurstFS (Wang et al. 2016). 
The system is created at the start of the calculation task and 
released at the end of the task. Several similar computing 
tasks can share the BurstFS service, thus reducing the bur­
den of the underlying parallel file system.
BurstFS uses MDHIM to build a distributed key value 
storage to manage metadata, and its servers are distributed 
on various computing nodes. In order to reduce the number 
of key value requests, BurstFS adopts a delayed synchro­
nization mechanism to consolidate continuous metadata 
operations. Unlike the write operation directly completed 
locally, BurstFS’s read operation is implemented through 
a mechanism called “Co-located I/O delegation”. Specifi­
cally, the I/O and computing processes are deployed on the 
same node. The computing process sends the I/O request to 
the agents on the same node, while the I/O agents on dif­
ferent nodes interact through point-to-point communication. 
The agent’s I/O management service will consolidate data 
requests as much as possible and streamline access opera­
tions to local storage. Based on this design, all write opera­
tions can be completed locally, while read operations are 
handled by I/O agents, thus avoiding intensive read access to 
the underlying parallel file system. BurstFS can be attached 
to a configurable path and intercept all POSIX operations 
under the path in a transparent manner to users.

4.3  Prospect
The implementation and value proposition of burst buffer 
can be analyzed across several dimensions. From a perfor­
mance perspective, they drastically reduce the time required 
for checkpointing, which is often the dominant I/O activity 
in HPC. This is achieved by writing data at the speed of 
local flash to the burst buffer, which then asynchronously 
stages it out to the PFS in the background. This decoupling 
leads to significant improvements in aggregate throughput 
and application scalability. In terms of data management, 
they enable in-situ data services such as in-transit process­
ing, where data is filtered, compressed, or reformatted 
before being committed to long-term storage, substantially 
reducing the final data volume. Early implementations like 
the Cray DataWarp and research prototypes like DeltaFS 
(Zheng et al. 2021) demonstrated the feasibility and benefits 
of this architecture. However, the adoption of burst buffer 
introduces trade-offs in complexity and cost. They add a 
new layer to the storage hierarchy that requires sophisticated 
software for data placement, lifecycle management, and 
namespace integration. Furthermore, the economic cost of 
deploying a large-scale flash-based tier is non-trivial, mak­
ing its return on investment a key consideration for system 
designers. The evolution of Burst Buffers is now converg­
ing with broader trends in composable infrastructure and the 
use of ZNS SSDs for more predictable performance, posi­
tioning them not just as a temporary cache, but as an intelli­
gent, programmable staging area for the exascale computing 
era (Koo et al. 2021).

5.2  NVMe-oF
With the advent of the era of big data, the real-time require­
ment of massive data processing urges the storage sys­
tem to have higher bandwidth and throughput. In order to 
meet this demand, data access protocols are also evolving, 
and NVMe-oF network storage is gradually becoming the 
development trend in the future. NVMe control protocol 
has gradually replaced the traditional SAS protocol by vir­
tue of its efficient concurrent communication ability with 
CPU. At the same time, the continuous maturity of RDMA 
and NVMe SSD technology has promoted the transforma­
tion of storage architecture. After entering the NVMe SSD 
era, the performance and life of storage media have been 
significantly improved compared with traditional HDDs, 
while CPU may become a new performance bottleneck. 
In this context, the traditional centralized and distributed 
(NVIDIA 2025a) are deeply integrated with InfiniBand 
and build low latency training clusters through Quantum-2 
switches. However, the cost of private network card and 
switch of InfiniBand is high, and its compatibility with Eth­
ernet ecosystem is weak, which increases the complexity 
of operation and maintenance. Japan’s Fugaku system uses 
InfiniBand technology to build a communication network 
between computing and storage.
RoCE is an Ethernet compatible alternative to Infini­
Band, which aims to reduce costs by reusing existing Eth­
ernet infrastructure. RoCEv2 supports IP routing and can 
achieve RDMA performance close to InfiniBand on stan­
dard Ethernet (latency 1 to 3 microseconds). Cloud service 
providers such as Microsoft Azure have widely used RoCE 
to build high performance cloud hosts. However, RoCE 
has high requirements for lossless networks. Priority flow 
control and explicit congestion notification need to be con­
figured to avoid congestion. Large scale deployment may 
face the risk of PFC storm, requiring fine network tuning. 
Huawei’s OceanStor high performance disk array (Huawei 
2025) fully supports the RoCE network and can provide 
excellent storage services for high performance computer 
systems.
PCIe, as the industry standard for interconnection of inter­
nal devices in servers, focuses on low latency and high band­
width of board level communication. PCIe 5.0 × 16 channel 
can provide two-way 128 GB/s bandwidth, and the latency 
is less than 100 ns. It is an ideal choice for GPU, FPGA 
accelerator card and NVMe SSD. For example, NVIDIA’s 
GPU works with NVLink through PCIe to achieve high-
speed data exchange within the computing node. However, 
the transmission distance of PCIe is limited to the inside 
of the chassis (usually less than 1 m), and the scalability is 
limited, so it cannot be directly used for cross node com­
munication. The more successful application example in the 
high performance storage system is El Capitan in Fig. 5. Its 
computing node is located in the same chassis as the rabbit 
node, which makes full use of the high bandwidth perfor­
mance of PCIe to expand the storage resources for comput­
ing nodes, and skillfully avoids the disadvantage that the 
PCIe link cannot transmit over a long distance.
Tradeoff between performance and cost: in terms of per­
formance, the four technologies show obvious ladder differ­
ences: Slingshot and InfiniBand focus on ultra-low latency 
and high throughput, which are suitable for HPC and AI 
scenarios that are extremely sensitive to network perfor­
mance; RoCE achieves a balance between Ethernet Com­
patibility and performance, and is suitable for cost sensitive 
scenarios; PCIe is the only choice for device level intercon­
nection with nanosecond latency and ultra-high bandwidth. 
However, performance advantages are often accompanied 
by rising costs—Slingshot’s proprietary hardware and

5.3  Prospect
The storage communication network has evolved from a 
passive data conduit into a critical, performance-defining 
component of the modern data center, directly influencing 
latency, throughput, and overall system scalability. Remote 
Direct Memory Access (RDMA) is the cornerstone of this 
transformation, enabling direct memory-to-memory data 
transfer between nodes with minimal CPU intervention. 
Protocols like RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) and 
InfiniBand leverage RDMA to deliver ultra-low latency and 
high bandwidth, which is indispensable for disaggregated 
storage architectures and latency-sensitive applications. 
However, the traditional kernel-based network and storage 
stack became a bottleneck, leading to the development of 
user-space frameworks. The Storage Performance Develop­
ment Kit (SPDK) (Ren and Trivedi 2023) exemplifies this 
shift, implementing a poll-mode, kernel-bypassing NVMe 
driver that eliminates context switch overheads and achieves 
unprecedented I/O rates. Complementarily, the Linux io_
uring asynchronous I/O interface provides a highly efficient 
mechanism for high-throughput storage communication 
within the kernel ecosystem, significantly reducing system 
call overhead and enabling true async I/O for both network 
and storage operations. The convergence of networking and 
storage protocols is most evident in NVMe over Fabrics

NVMe-oF protocol defines how to realize NVMe function 
through various general transport protocols. The emergence 
of NVMe-oF not only solves the performance bottleneck 
of existing protocols, but also allows organizations to build 
highly distributed, highly available and horizontally scal­
able storage architectures. By extending the NVMe protocol 
to SAN (storage area network) devices, NVMe-oF improves 
CPU efficiency and speeds up the connection between serv­
ers and storage applications.
NVMe-oF mainly supports three types of fabric transmis­
sion options, namely FC (fibre channel), RDMA and TCP. 
RDMA supports InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP. NVMe-
oF/RDMA makes use of the advantages of RDMA network 
and becomes an ideal fabric transport layer protocol. It pro­
vides transmission with low latency, low jitter and low CPU 
utilization. It can maximize the use of hardware acceleration 
and avoid the overhead of software protocol stack. In addi­
tion, because RDMA is a memory read–write technology, 
it can also be applied to a variety of scenarios, such as the 
GPU direct storage technology proposed by NVIDIA, which 
allows GPU to bypass the CPU and directly access storage 
devices. RDMA is its foundation. NVMe-oF/TCP makes 
use of the reliable transmission characteristics of TCP pro­
tocol, the universality and good interoperability of TCP/IP 
network, and is suitable for modern data center network. In 
scenarios where performance requirements are not particu­
larly high, NVMe-oF/TCP can be used as an alternative.

to be compatible with the mixed deployment mode, support­
ing elastic expansion and multi-tenant isolation, which puts 
forward higher requirements for the flexibility and security of 
the storage architecture.
Besides, the rise of LLMs (large language models) and 
multimodal applications demands a fundamental shift in 
high-performance storage, moving beyond raw through­
put to prioritize extreme low-latency and massive IOPS for 
small, random reads (Pan et al. 2025; Gptcache 2023). The 
entire AI lifecycle, from training on vast datasets to the rapid 
token generation of inference, creates immense pressure, 
requiring storage to handle both massive sequential work­
loads and millions of concurrent small files. Multimodal 
data adds complexity, necessitating synchronized access 
across diverse data types. The core challenge is building a 
scalable, parallel storage fabric that eliminates I/O bottle­
necks, preventing storage from becoming the critical path 
in AI development.
In a word, the future development of high performance 
storage system needs to take “performance-cost-energy-effi­
ciency” collaborative optimization as the core, and build an 
intelligent storage infrastructure to support the data flood in ZB 
era through interdisciplinary integration and software and hard­
ware collaborative innovation. Only by continuously breaking 
through the limits of media, reconstructing network topology, 
and deepening AI empowerment, can we truly bridge the per­
formance gap between storage and computing, and provide a 
solid data foundation for cutting-edge fields such as exascale 
computing, cognitive science, and quantum simulation.

6  Summary and prospect
At present, the innovation of high performance storage system 
in the fields of architecture, hardware, software and network 
communication has significantly alleviated the data flood 
pressure brought by exascale computing. The storage com­
puting separation and distributed architecture effectively bal­
ances scalability and performance requirements by decoupling 
computing and storage resources and combining hierarchical 
design (such as I/O forwarding layer and near-computing stor­
age layer). The supercomputing system represented by Frontier 
and Fugaku has verified the feasibility of this kind of architec­
ture. It uses hardware acceleration technologies such as local 
NVMe SSD and persistent memory to increase the storage 
bandwidth to TB/s level, and optimizes metadata management 
and hybrid load scheduling with the help of parallel file systems 
such as Lustre and DAOS. The breakthrough of storage net­
work communication technology (such as Slingshot and CXL) 
further reduces the cross node access latency, and provides a 
physical basis for storage computing collaboration. However, 
the existing technology still faces the trade-off between cost 
and performance. The high power consumption, high cost, 
synchronization overhead of distributed metadata and the com­
plexity of cross level data scheduling of all flash arrays restrict 
the energy efficiency and intelligent level of storage systems.
Facing the future, the evolution of high performance storage 
systems will present three major trends. First, at the hardware 
level, the storage-computing integrated architecture and new 
media will be deeply integrated. For example, the memory 
pooling technology based on CXL protocol can break the 
“memory wall” limit. Photonic interconnection and storage-
computing chips are expected to reduce the storage network 
latency to nanosecond level and improve energy efficiency. 
Second, the software ecosystem will transform to the direction 
of AI native and adaptive, dynamically predict the I/O mode 
through machine learning, optimize the data layout, and build 
an intelligent cache strategy to deal with the highly dynamic 
load characteristics in AI training and scientific computing.

Abstract: As high performance computing (HPC) moves towards exascale, storage systems face core challenges such as data flood­ ing, bandwidth bottlenecks, mixed load coordination, and performance cost balancing. This article systematically reviews the cutting-edge technologies of high performance storage systems, covering four aspects: storage architecture, hardware, software, and networking. At the architecture level, storage computing separation, distributed and hierarchical architec­ tures decouple computing and storage resources, and optimize latency and scalability through high-speed networks. Typi­ cal cases include supercomputer systems such as Frontier and Fugaku. In terms of hardware, persistent memory, all flash array, and integrated storage and computing chips significantly improve throughput and reduce latency, while ZNS SSD and QLC technology optimize cost and lifespan. At the software level, distributed parallel file systems respond to mas­ sive small files and high concurrency access through burst buffering technology. In network communication, low latency protocols such as Slingshot, InfiniBand, and RoCE support TB level bandwidth, while CXL technology promotes storage resource pooling. In the future, photon interconnection, AI native architecture, and green energy-saving technologies will further promote the development of high performance storage towards efficiency and intelligence, to support ZB level storage requirements in scenarios such as Exascale computing and AI training.
